title: The sunnah prayers
hook: regular extra units before and after the obligatory ones

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iqamah, and your line: stand now. Did you step into something calmly when it finally began? Before the iqamah, there was a space for a prayer. Today, what fills it. Day one thousand eighty.

Better than the world and everything in it. That's a big claim to make about two short units of prayer, said quietly in a dark bedroom before the dawn prayer, with the alarm still blinking and nobody watching. Aishah reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying exactly that about the two units before the dawn prayer, in Sahih Muslim, number 725. Not the obligatory prayer. The small extra one before it. Today, the prayers that sit around the obligatory ones like a frame around a picture.
screen: `BETTER THAN THE WORLD.` → `TWO SHORT UNITS, BEFORE DAWN.` → `A FRAME AROUND A PICTURE.`

segments.voice: The word is rawatib, the regular ones. They're the voluntary prayers the Prophet ﷺ kept attached to the obligatory prayers, some just before, some just after. Not required. But not random either. In Sahih Muslim, number 728, his wife Umm Habibah reports him saying that whoever prays twelve units a day and night, beyond the obligatory, will have a house built for them in the garden. And Umm Habibah adds that she never stopped praying them after she heard it. Jami at-Tirmidhi, number 415, lays out where those units fall: four before the noon prayer and two after it, two after the sunset prayer, two after the night prayer, and two before dawn. Another companion, Ibn Umar, in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 1180, remembers ten, with two before noon instead of four. The schools follow these reports in slightly different ways, and Shia practice keeps its own pattern of daily voluntary prayers. And among all of them, one pair gets special weight. Aishah says, in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 1169, that the Prophet ﷺ was not more careful about any voluntary prayer than the two before dawn. Why pray what isn't required? One answer is in the word sunnah itself: following how he actually prayed, not only what was demanded. Another is in a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 864: on the day of reckoning, if the obligatory prayers fall short, the voluntary ones are looked to, to make up what's missing. The frame protects the picture.
screen: `RAWATIB: THE REGULAR ONES.` · `UMM HABIBAH: TWELVE, A HOUSE IN THE GARDEN.` · `THE TWO BEFORE DAWN, KEPT MOST CAREFULLY.` · `THE FRAME PROTECTS THE PICTURE.` · then, large: `BETTER THAN THE WORLD AND ALL IN IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: add two before dawn. Not now, but plan it now. Settle, and breathe. Picture tomorrow morning: the alarm, the dark, the minute before the dawn prayer or before your day begins. See yourself adding something small and extra there, before the main thing. If you pray, those are the two units before fajr; you can decide now that tomorrow you'll pray them. If you don't, choose a two-minute habit to set before the first big task of your day. Then sit quietly with the decision made. The bell holds the time.
Rawatib. The regular voluntary prayers, before and after the obligatory ones, with the two before dawn kept most carefully of all. Today's word.
Your line: the sunnah around it. Today, put one small extra thing just before or after something you have to do, and see how it changes it. Tomorrow, the odd prayer. Day one thousand eighty.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep the rawatib pray short voluntary units before or after the obligatory prayers, at home or in the mosque, following the pattern their school teaches, and give particular care to the two units before the dawn prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: extra prayers are for the extra devout.
what it means: a regular frame of voluntary units around the obligatory prayers, kept by the Prophet.
what a scholar hears: twelve in Umm Habibah's report, ten in Ibn Umar's, and Abu Dawud 864 on voluntary prayer making up what the obligatory lacks.

notes: Hadith numbers and details to confirm: Muslim 725 (Aishah: the two rak'ahs of fajr are better than the world and what is in it); Muslim 728 (Umm Habibah: twelve rak'ahs, a house in Paradise; 'I have not left them since'); Tirmidhi 415 (the distribution of the twelve); Bukhari 1180 (Ibn 'Umar's ten); Bukhari 1169 (Aishah: none more regular than the two before fajr); Abu Dawud 864 (voluntary prayers make up for deficient obligatory ones).
Shia practice (the daily nawafil, with a different count) is mentioned only as 'its own pattern'; Keeper may add detail.
'Sunnah prayers' and 'rawatib' are used as near-synonyms per the index; strictly, sunnah prayers is broader.
